conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the focus of public health, and at what level do its tools work?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Public health concerns the health of populations, not individuals — its tools work at the level of communities and systems rather than one patient.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the three pillars of public health, and what is the organising spine?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Prevention & screening; health promotion; the determinants of health — the organising spine is the levels of prevention, into which all three slot.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is primordial prevention — its aim and examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Aim: prevent the risk factors arising. Examples: population policy — sugar tax, clean air, urban planning.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is primary prevention — its aim and examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Aim: prevent disease before it occurs. Examples: vaccination, smoking cessation, health promotion.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is secondary prevention — its aim and key example?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Aim: detect early/pre-symptomatic disease. Key example: screening.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is tertiary prevention — its aim and examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Aim: limit damage/complications of established disease. Examples: rehabilitation, secondary-prevention drugs (statins post-MI).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the anchor linking screening to the levels of prevention?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Screening = secondary prevention (catching disease in its latent/early stage).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the definition of screening, and what does a screen-positive result mean?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Testing asymptomatic people to detect disease (or risk) at an early, more treatable stage. A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the Wilson-Jungner criteria relating to 'the condition'?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Important health problem; recognisable latent/early stage; natural history understood.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the Wilson-Jungner criteria relating to 'the test'?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Suitable, acceptable, sensitive + specific, safe.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the Wilson-Jungner criteria relating to 'the treatment'?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Effective treatment exists; agreed policy on whom to treat; facilities available.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the Wilson-Jungner criteria relating to 'the programme'?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Cost-effective; continuous/ongoing (not one-off); benefit outweighs harm.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK AAA screening programme — who, test and interval?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: men in the year they turn 65. Test: abdominal USS. Interval: one-off.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK breast cancer screening programme — who, test and interval?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: women 50-70 (self-refer >70). Test: mammogram. Interval: 3-yearly.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK cervical screening programme — who, test and interval?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: women/people with a cervix 25-64. Test: HPV-primary smear. Interval: now 5-yearly for HPV-negative results at all ages 25-64 (England moved 25-49 from 3- to 5-yearly in July 2025; Scotland/Wales earlier). HPV-positive results get earlier recall/colposcopy.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK bowel cancer screening programme — who, test and interval?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: everyone 50-74. Test: FIT home kit. Interval: 2-yearly.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK diabetic eye screening programme — who, test and interval?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: diabetics aged ≥12. Test: retinal photography. Interval: annually.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the UK antenatal/newborn screening programme — who and tests?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who: pregnancy + newborns. Tests: bloods/USS, NIPE, blood spot, hearing.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is lead-time bias in screening?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Screening detects disease earlier → survival appears longer, but only because the clock started earlier — death isn't actually delayed.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is length-time bias in screening?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Screening preferentially catches slow-growing (better-prognosis) disease; fast aggressive disease presents symptomatically between screens.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is overdiagnosis in screening?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Detecting disease that would never have caused harm → unnecessary treatment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is selection (healthy-volunteer) bias in screening?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Those who attend screening are healthier than those who don't.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the harms of screening (it's not free)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: False positives (anxiety, unnecessary invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), and overdiagnosis/overtreatment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the definition of health promotion?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Enabling people to increase control over and improve their health — broader than just giving information.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the difference between health education and health promotion?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Education = providing information/knowledge; promotion = the wider effort including policy, environment, and enabling change.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the five action areas of the Ottawa Charter?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Build healthy public policy; create supportive environments; strengthen community action; develop personal skills; reorient health services.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What levels do health-promotion approaches span?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Individual (advice, brief interventions), community (programmes), and population/policy (legislation, taxation — 'nudge').

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the core idea about the determinants of health?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Health is determined far more by social, economic, and environmental factors than by healthcare itself — most variation in population health lies outside the clinic.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the layers of the Dahlgren-Whitehead 'rainbow' model (innermost → outermost)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Age, sex, genetics (fixed, innermost); individual lifestyle factors (smoking, diet, exercise); social + community networks (family, friends, support); living + working conditions (housing, education, employment, healthcare access, food); general socioeconomic, cultural + environmental conditions (outermost).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the social determinants of health (SDOH)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age — income, education, housing, employment, environment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are health inequalities and the social gradient (Marmot)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Health follows a gradient — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health, stepwise across the whole of society (not just rich vs poor). Marmot's principle: 'the causes of the causes'.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the difference between equality and equity, and which is the more relevant public-health goal?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Equality = everyone gets the same; equity = allocation according to need (the more relevant public-health goal).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Define life expectancy and healthy life expectancy.
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Life expectancy: years a person can expect to live from birth if conditions stayed the same. Healthy life expectancy: years expected to live in self-assessed good health.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Define amenable mortality and mortality rate.
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Amenable mortality: premature deaths that adequate healthcare could have prevented. Mortality rate: deaths per year per 100,000 — affected by healthcare, social, economic + environmental factors.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the four levels of prevention, with their aims and examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Primordial: prevent the risk factors arising — population policy (sugar tax, clean air, urban planning). Primary: prevent disease before it occurs — vaccination, smoking cessation, health promotion. Secondary: detect early/pre-symptomatic disease — screening. Tertiary: limit damage/complications of established disease — rehabilitation, secondary-prevention drugs (statins post-MI).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which level of prevention is screening, and why?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Screening = secondary prevention (catching disease in its latent/early stage).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is screening, and why is a screen-positive result not a diagnosis?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Testing asymptomatic people to detect disease (or risk) at an early, more treatable stage. A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is health promotion, and how does it differ from health education?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Enabling people to increase control over and improve their health — broader than just giving information. Health education = providing information/knowledge; health promotion = the wider effort including policy, environment, and enabling change.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the social gradient (Marmot), and what is Marmot's principle?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Health follows a gradient — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health, stepwise across the whole of society (not just rich vs poor). Marmot's principle: 'the causes of the causes'.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the difference between equality and equity?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Equality = everyone gets the same; equity = allocation according to need (the more relevant public-health goal).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is evidence-based medicine (EBM)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Integrating the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the two halves of EBM?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The EBM framework (hierarchy of evidence, study designs, appraisal) and the medical statistics (diagnostic-test maths, measures of effect, significance).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the hierarchy of evidence (the EBM pyramid), from strongest to weakest?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: 1 (top, strongest): systematic reviews + meta-analyses of RCTs. 2: randomised controlled trials (RCTs). 3: cohort studies. 4: case-control studies. 5: case series / case reports. 6 (bottom, weakest): expert opinion.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Why do systematic reviews/meta-analyses sit at the top of the evidence hierarchy?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Higher = less bias, more reliable; systematic review/meta-analysis sits at the top by pooling all relevant studies.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is an RCT — its direction, measures, and what it's best for?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Prospective, randomised + controlled; measures RR, ARR, NNT; best for establishing causation (gold standard for interventions).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a cohort study — its direction, measure, and what it's best for?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Prospective — follow exposed vs unexposed forward; measures relative risk (RR), incidence; best for risk factors, prognosis (good for common outcomes).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a case-control study — its direction, measure, and what it's best for?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Retrospective — cases vs controls, look back; measures the odds ratio (OR); best for rare diseases, quick/cheap.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a cross-sectional study — its direction, measure, and what it's best for?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: A snapshot in time; measures prevalence; best for prevalence surveys.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is an ecological study?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Population-level; hypothesis-generating.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the difference between parallel and crossover trial structures?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Parallel: groups run concurrently. Crossover: each patient gets both treatments sequentially — acting as their own control. RR for cohort, OR for case-control is the key pairing.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: In a diagnostic 2×2 table, what are the four cells?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Test + / Disease +: true positive (TP). Test + / Disease −: false positive (FP). Test − / Disease +: false negative (FN). Test − / Disease −: true negative (TN).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is sensitivity — its formula and meaning?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: TP / (TP+FN). Of those with disease, the proportion testing positive (intrinsic).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is specificity — its formula and meaning?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: TN / (TN+FP). Of those without disease, the proportion testing negative (intrinsic).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is positive predictive value (PPV) — its formula and meaning?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: TP / (TP+FP). Of those testing positive, the proportion who truly have disease (prevalence-dependent).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is negative predictive value (NPV) — its formula and meaning?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: TN / (TN+FN). Of those testing negative, the proportion truly disease-free (prevalence-dependent).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the two rules SnNOut and SpPIn?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: SnNOut — a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules Out disease (good for screening). SpPIn — a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules In disease (good for confirmation).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the prevalence point regarding sensitivity/specificity vs PPV/NPV?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Sensitivity + specificity are intrinsic (don't change with prevalence); PPV + NPV depend on prevalence — as prevalence falls, PPV falls (more false positives relative to true). This is why screening low-prevalence populations generates many false positives.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the likelihood ratios, and their formulas?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Likelihood ratios are prevalence-independent. LR+ = sens/(1−spec) (>10 = strong rule-in); LR− = (1−sens)/spec (<0.1 = strong rule-out).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is relative risk (RR) — its meaning and interpretation?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; RR >1 = ↑risk, <1 = protective (cohort/RCT).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the odds ratio (OR) — its meaning?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Odds of exposure in cases ÷ controls (case-control; approximates RR for rare disease).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is absolute risk reduction (ARR)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Control event rate − treatment event rate.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is number needed to treat (NNT)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: 1 / ARR — the number of patients treated to prevent one outcome (lower = better).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is number needed to harm (NNH)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: 1 / absolute risk increase (higher = safer).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is relative risk reduction (RRR), and why watch out for it?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Proportional reduction — can look impressive while the ARR is tiny (the 'spin' to watch).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a p-value?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The probability the result (or more extreme) occurred by chance if the null were true; <0.05 = 'statistically significant' (an arbitrary threshold).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a confidence interval (CI), and when does it indicate non-significance?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The range within which the true value lies (usually 95%); narrow = precise. If a 95% CI for RR/OR crosses 1 (or a difference crosses 0) → not significant.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a type I error (α)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: False positive — rejecting a true null (concluding an effect that isn't real).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is a type II error (β), and how does power relate?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: False negative — missing a real effect; power = 1−β (increased by a larger sample size).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the null hypothesis?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The hypothesis of 'no difference/effect'.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Why is a confidence interval more informative than a p-value alone?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: A CI conveys both significance and precision/effect size — more informative than p alone.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is bias (systematic error), and what are examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Systematic error. Examples: selection bias (incl. healthy-volunteer), information/measurement bias, recall bias (case-control), observer bias (→ blinding), lead-time + length-time bias (screening), attrition bias (dropouts).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is confounding, and how is it controlled?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: A third factor associated with both exposure and outcome, distorting the link (e.g. age, smoking) — controlled by randomisation, matching, restriction, multivariable adjustment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: How is bias reduced in RCTs?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Randomisation (balances confounders), blinding (single/double), allocation concealment, intention-to-treat analysis.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the 5 A's of the EBM process?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Ask (form a focused PICO question — Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) → Acquire (search) → Appraise (critically appraise validity — CASP checklists) → Apply (to the patient, with their values) → Assess (evaluate outcome).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What does critical appraisal ask?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Are the results valid (bias/confounding?), important (effect size/CI?), and applicable (to my patient?).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the notifiable diseases framework, and what is its purpose?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: A public-health framework, not a disease note: the legal duty to report specified infectious diseases to public health authorities so they can act to protect the population.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the core principle of notification, and why does timing matter?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: You notify on clinical suspicion alone — do not wait for laboratory confirmation, as that delays the public-health response.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What are the three things examined about notifiable diseases?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Who notifies whom, the timing, and why (plus recognising which diseases are notifiable).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Who has the duty to notify, and on what grounds?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) — any GMC-registered doctor — with 'reasonable grounds for suspecting' a notifiable disease.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: To whom is a notifiable disease reported?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The 'Proper Officer' of the local authority (in practice, the local UKHSA Health Protection Team).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the legal basis for notification, and is it optional?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 — a statutory duty, not optional.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the parallel laboratory duty, and does it remove the doctor's duty?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Diagnostic labs have a separate statutory duty to report the isolation of specific notifiable organisms (e.g. Neisseria meningitidis from a blood culture). A lab report does NOT remove the doctor's duty to notify on clinical suspicion — the two systems complement each other.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: How and when are URGENT notifiable cases reported, with examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: How: telephone the HPT. When: within 24 hours. Examples: meningococcal disease, measles, food-poisoning outbreaks.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: How and when are ROUTINE notifiable cases reported, with examples?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: How: online / written notification form. When: within 3 days. Examples: TB, mumps, scarlet fever.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Why are urgent cases phoned within 24 h, and what must all cases still do?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Urgent cases are phoned within 24 h because there is often a critical window for control measures; all cases (including urgent) also need the written/online form within 3 days.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the golden rule of notification timing?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Notify on clinical suspicion — do not wait for lab confirmation.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: How long is the full statutory notifiable list, and what is the realistic expectation?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The full statutory list is ~30+; the realistic expectation is to recognise a disease as notifiable and know the high-yield ones.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which notifiable diseases are the vaccine-preventable / childhood group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis (whooping cough), diphtheria, tetanus, polio (acute poliomyelitis).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which notifiable diseases are in the severe bacterial / toxin group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Meningococcal septicaemia, scarlet fever, diphtheria, tetanus, anthrax, botulism, plague.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which notifiable diseases are in the GI / food & water group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Food poisoning, cholera, typhoid & paratyphoid (enteric fever), dysentery, acute hepatitis A-E.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which notifiable diseases are in the respiratory / environmental group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: TB, Legionnaires' disease, SARS, COVID-19, invasive group A strep.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which notifiable diseases are in the zoonotic / imported / tropical group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Rabies, malaria, viral haemorrhagic fevers (Ebola etc.), brucellosis, leptospirosis, yellow fever, typhus.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the 'definitely know these' high-yield notifiable subset?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Measles, meningococcal disease, food poisoning, TB, mumps, scarlet fever, COVID-19 — focus on the urgent ones and the common routine ones.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Which infections are NON-notifiable (the classic trap)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: MRSA / Staph aureus, C. difficile, CJD have separate surveillance, not statutory notification. HIV is also NOT statutorily notifiable (confidential surveillance).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the 'all-hazards' catch-all principle, and what does it cover?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The duty isn't limited to the listed diseases: an RMP should notify any infection or contamination (including non-listed/emerging infections, and chemical/radiation hazards) that presents, or could present, significant harm to human health — e.g. a novel pathogen, a cluster, or carbon monoxide poisoning.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Give an example of the 'all-hazards' principle in action beyond the formal list.
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Notifying parvovirus B19 in a contact of a pregnant woman, even though it's not on the formal list.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What is the public-health rationale for notification (why notify)?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Surveillance (tracking incidence and trends), outbreak detection, contact tracing, and implementing control measures to prevent further spread.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What do notifications trigger once received?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Some notifications trigger immediate public-health action — antibiotics, vaccination, or isolation advice for contacts; others strengthen surveillance and let UKHSA assess interventions like vaccine programmes.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: What happens after notification to break the chain of transmission?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: Contact tracing (identifying and monitoring close contacts); prophylaxis — vaccination or antibiotics for contacts (e.g. ciprofloxacin for meningococcal contacts); environmental investigation — water systems for Legionella, premises for food poisoning.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.front: Who takes over the epidemiological work after notification, and what is the doctor's job?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.back: The HPT takes over the epidemiological work; the doctor's job is the prompt, suspicion-based notification.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What distinguishes public health from individual clinical practice?
options: It concerns the health of individuals at the bedside
It concerns the health of populations, working at the level of communities and systems rather than one patient
It only deals with infectious diseases
It is limited to hospital care
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: It concerns the health of populations, working at the level of communities and systems rather than one patient
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Public health concerns the health of populations, not individuals, with its tools working at the level of communities and systems rather than one patient.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Childhood vaccination and smoking cessation are examples of which level of prevention?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Primary prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Primary prevention aims to prevent disease before it occurs, with examples including vaccination, smoking cessation and health promotion.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A sugar tax and clean-air urban planning are best classified as which level of prevention?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Primordial prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Primordial prevention aims to prevent the risk factors arising, through population policy such as a sugar tax, clean air and urban planning.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Screening fits into which level of prevention, and why?
options: Primary, because it prevents disease occurring
Secondary, because it detects early/pre-symptomatic disease in its latent/early stage
Tertiary, because it limits complications of established disease
Primordial, because it prevents risk factors
It is not a form of prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Secondary, because it detects early/pre-symptomatic disease in its latent/early stage
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Screening is secondary prevention — detecting early/pre-symptomatic disease and catching it in its latent/early stage.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Giving statins after a myocardial infarction and rehabilitation are examples of which level of prevention?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Tertiary prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Tertiary prevention limits damage/complications of established disease, with examples including rehabilitation and secondary-prevention drugs such as statins post-MI.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A patient receives a screen-positive result. What does this mean?
options: The patient definitely has the disease
It is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test
The patient should start treatment immediately without further tests
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: It is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Screening tests asymptomatic people to detect disease or risk at an early, more treatable stage; a screen-positive result is not a diagnosis and triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Under the Wilson-Jungner criteria, which statement about 'the condition' is correct?
options: It should be rare and untreatable
It should be an important health problem with a recognisable latent/early stage and an understood natural history
Its natural history can be unknown
It need not have an early stage
It should have no available treatment
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: It should be an important health problem with a recognisable latent/early stage and an understood natural history
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Wilson-Jungner criteria for the condition: it should be an important health problem, have a recognisable latent/early stage, and have an understood natural history.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which set of features describes 'the test' under the Wilson-Jungner criteria?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Suitable, acceptable, sensitive + specific, safe
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Under Wilson-Jungner, the test should be suitable, acceptable, sensitive and specific, and safe.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which Wilson-Jungner criterion applies to 'the programme'?
options: It should be a one-off rather than ongoing
It should be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing (not one-off), and its benefit should outweigh harm
Harm may outweigh benefit if uptake is high
It applies only to symptomatic people
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: It should be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing (not one-off), and its benefit should outweigh harm
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Under Wilson-Jungner, the programme should be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing (not one-off), and its benefit should outweigh harm.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Who is invited for AAA screening in the UK, and what test is used?
options: Men in the year they turn 65; abdominal ultrasound, as a one-off
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Men in the year they turn 65; abdominal ultrasound, as a one-off
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The UK AAA programme screens men in the year they turn 65 with a one-off abdominal ultrasound.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the UK cervical screening test and interval for women aged 25-49?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: HPV-primary smear, 5-yearly (if HPV negative)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: UK cervical screening uses HPV-primary testing in women/people with a cervix aged 25-64. Following the move to a longer interval for HPV-negative results (Wales/Scotland, then NHS England from 2025), the routine recall is now 5-yearly for ages 25-49 (previously 3-yearly) and remains 5-yearly for 50-64. HPV-positive samples are recalled sooner (reflex cytology, 12-month repeat, or colposcopy).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which UK screening programme uses a FIT home kit, and for whom?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Bowel screening; everyone 50-74, 2-yearly
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: UK bowel cancer screening uses a FIT home kit for everyone aged 50-74, 2-yearly.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How often is diabetic eye screening performed, and for whom?
options: Annually; diabetics aged ≥12, using retinal photography
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Annually; diabetics aged ≥12, using retinal photography
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: UK diabetic eye screening is performed annually in diabetics aged ≥12 using retinal photography.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A screening study reports longer survival from diagnosis, but the actual time of death is unchanged. Which bias does this describe?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Lead-time bias
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Lead-time bias: screening detects disease earlier so survival appears longer, but only because the clock started earlier — death isn't actually delayed.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Screening tends to pick up indolent, slow-growing tumours while aggressive cancers surface symptomatically between screens. Which bias is this?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Length-time bias
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Length-time bias: screening preferentially catches slow-growing (better-prognosis) disease, while fast aggressive disease presents symptomatically between screens.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Detecting disease that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment, is termed:
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Overdiagnosis
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Overdiagnosis is detecting disease that would never have caused harm, leading to unnecessary treatment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What are recognised harms of screening?
options: There are no harms — screening is always beneficial
False positives (anxiety, unnecessary invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), and overdiagnosis/overtreatment
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: False positives (anxiety, unnecessary invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), and overdiagnosis/overtreatment
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Screening is not free of harm: it can cause false positives (anxiety, unnecessary invasive tests), false negatives (false reassurance), and overdiagnosis/overtreatment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How does health education differ from health promotion?
options: Education is providing information/knowledge, whereas promotion is the wider effort including policy, environment and enabling change
Promotion is only giving information; education is the wider effort
Education includes legislation; promotion does not
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Education is providing information/knowledge, whereas promotion is the wider effort including policy, environment and enabling change
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Health education is providing information/knowledge, while health promotion is the wider effort — enabling people to increase control over and improve their health — including policy, environment and enabling change.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of the following is one of the five action areas of the Ottawa Charter?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Build healthy public policy
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The Ottawa Charter's five action areas are: build healthy public policy, create supportive environments, strengthen community action, develop personal skills, and reorient health services.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the core idea about the determinants of health?
options: Health is determined mainly by healthcare access
Health is determined far more by social, economic and environmental factors than by healthcare itself — most variation in population health lies outside the clinic
Healthcare explains all variation in health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Health is determined far more by social, economic and environmental factors than by healthcare itself — most variation in population health lies outside the clinic
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The core idea is that health is determined far more by social, economic and environmental factors than by healthcare itself, with most variation in population health lying outside the clinic.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: In the Dahlgren-Whitehead 'rainbow' model, which factors form the fixed, innermost layer?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Age, sex and genetics
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: In the Dahlgren-Whitehead model, age, sex and genetics form the fixed, innermost layer, surrounded outward by lifestyle factors, social/community networks, living/working conditions, and general socioeconomic/cultural/environmental conditions.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What does the Marmot social gradient describe, and what is its associated principle?
options: Health only differs between the very rich and very poor; 'survival of the fittest'
Health follows a stepwise gradient across the whole of society — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health; the principle is 'the causes of the causes'
Health is unrelated to socioeconomic position
Only genetics determines the gradient; 'nature over nurture'
The gradient applies only to infectious disease
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Health follows a stepwise gradient across the whole of society — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health; the principle is 'the causes of the causes'
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The Marmot social gradient describes how health follows a stepwise gradient across the whole of society (not just rich vs poor) — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health — with the principle 'the causes of the causes'.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the difference between equality and equity, and which is the more relevant public-health goal?
options: Equality = allocation by need; equity = everyone gets the same; equality is the goal
Equality = everyone gets the same; equity = allocation according to need; equity is the more relevant public-health goal
Equity means ignoring need; equality is the goal
Equality means allocation by need; neither is a goal
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Equality = everyone gets the same; equity = allocation according to need; equity is the more relevant public-health goal
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Equality means everyone gets the same, whereas equity means allocation according to need — equity being the more relevant public-health goal.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which population health measure is defined as premature deaths that adequate healthcare could have prevented?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Amenable mortality
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Amenable mortality is defined as premature deaths that adequate healthcare could have prevented.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What does 'healthy life expectancy' measure?
options: Years a person can expect to live from birth if conditions stayed the same
Years expected to live in self-assessed good health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Years expected to live in self-assessed good health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Healthy life expectancy is the years expected to live in self-assessed good health, in contrast to life expectancy (years a person can expect to live from birth if conditions stayed the same).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A sugar tax and clean-air legislation aim to stop risk factors from arising in the first place. Which level of prevention does this represent?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Primordial prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Primordial prevention aims to prevent the risk factors themselves from arising, through population policy such as a sugar tax, clean air, and urban planning.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which level of prevention does screening represent, and why?
options: Primary prevention — preventing disease before it occurs
Tertiary prevention — limiting complications of established disease
It is not a form of prevention
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Secondary prevention — detecting early/pre-symptomatic disease
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Screening is secondary prevention — it detects disease at an early/pre-symptomatic (latent) stage, catching it before symptoms occur.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A patient receives a positive screening result. What is the correct interpretation?
options: It confirms the diagnosis and treatment should begin
A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test
It means the person definitely does not have the disease
It is equivalent to a diagnostic test
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: A screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Screening tests asymptomatic people to detect disease early, but a screen-positive result is not a diagnosis — it triggers a confirmatory diagnostic test.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of the following is a Wilson-Jungner requirement for a screening programme (as opposed to the test or treatment)?
options: The test must be sensitive and specific
The programme must be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing, and its benefit must outweigh harm
The condition must have a latent stage
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The programme must be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing, and its benefit must outweigh harm
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The programme criteria require it to be cost-effective, continuous/ongoing (not one-off), with benefit outweighing harm. (Sensitivity/specificity and acceptability relate to the test; effective treatment relates to the treatment.)

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: The UK bowel cancer screening programme uses which test and interval?
options: FIT home kit, 2-yearly, for everyone aged 50–74
FIT home kit, annually, for over-60s only
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: FIT home kit, 2-yearly, for everyone aged 50–74
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: UK bowel screening offers a FIT home kit, 2-yearly, to everyone aged 50–74.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A screening study reports that screen-detected cancers have longer survival from diagnosis, but this is only because the disease was found earlier without death being delayed. What bias is this?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Lead-time bias
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Lead-time bias: screening detects disease earlier so survival appears longer, but only because the clock started earlier — death isn't actually delayed.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A screening programme appears to improve outcomes partly because it preferentially detects slow-growing, better-prognosis disease, while aggressive tumours present symptomatically between screens. What bias is this?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Length-time bias
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Length-time bias: screening preferentially catches slow-growing (better-prognosis) disease, whereas fast, aggressive disease presents symptomatically between screens.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A screening programme detects some cancers that would never have caused harm in the patient's lifetime, leading to unnecessary treatment. What is this called?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Overdiagnosis
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Overdiagnosis is detecting disease that would never have caused harm, resulting in unnecessary treatment — one of the recognised harms of screening.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which statement best distinguishes health education from health promotion?
options: Health education is providing information/knowledge; health promotion is the wider effort including policy, environment, and enabling change
Health promotion is only giving leaflets; education changes policy
Health education operates only at population level
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Health education is providing information/knowledge; health promotion is the wider effort including policy, environment, and enabling change
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Health education = providing information/knowledge, whereas health promotion is the broader effort of enabling people to increase control over and improve their health, including policy, environment, and enabling change.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Marmot's social gradient of health describes which pattern?
options: Health is only worse in the very poorest, with no effect elsewhere
Health follows a stepwise gradient across the whole of society — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health
Health is unrelated to socioeconomic position
The richest have the worst health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Health follows a stepwise gradient across the whole of society — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The Marmot social gradient shows health follows a gradient — the lower the socioeconomic position, the worse the health, stepwise across the whole of society (not just rich vs poor). Marmot's principle is 'the causes of the causes'.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of the following best defines evidence-based medicine?
options: Integrating the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions
Applying research findings without regard to individual patients
Relying solely on randomised controlled trials
Using only the cheapest available treatments
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Integrating the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: EBM is the integration of the best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values to guide decisions.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which study type sits at the top of the hierarchy of evidence?
options: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs sit at the top (strongest) of the evidence pyramid, because they pool all relevant studies — higher means less bias and more reliable. Expert opinion is weakest.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A researcher wants to study a rare disease quickly and cheaply. Which study design is most appropriate, and which measure of effect does it produce?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Case-control study; odds ratio
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: A case-control study (retrospective — cases vs controls, looking back) is best for rare diseases and is quick/cheap. It produces an odds ratio (OR), which approximates the RR for rare diseases.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which study design is the gold standard for establishing causation for an intervention?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Randomised controlled trial (RCT)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The RCT (prospective, randomised + controlled) is the gold standard for establishing causation for interventions, and measures RR, ARR and NNT.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A prospective study follows exposed and unexposed groups forward to assess a common outcome. What design is this, and what measure does it yield?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Cohort; relative risk and incidence
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: A cohort study is prospective — following exposed vs unexposed forward — and is good for risk factors and prognosis (common outcomes), yielding relative risk (RR) and incidence.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How is sensitivity calculated, and what does it mean?
options: TN/(TN+FP); of those without disease, the proportion testing negative
TP/(TP+FN); of those with disease, the proportion testing positive
TP/(TP+FP); of those testing positive, the proportion with disease
TN/(TN+FN); of those testing negative, the proportion disease-free
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: TP/(TP+FN); of those with disease, the proportion testing positive
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN) — of those with disease, the proportion testing positive. It is an intrinsic property that does not change with prevalence.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which value is prevalence-dependent rather than intrinsic to the test?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Positive predictive value (PPV)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: PPV (and NPV) depend on prevalence, whereas sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic. Likelihood ratios are prevalence-independent. As prevalence falls, PPV falls (more false positives relative to true).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A highly sensitive test is negative in a patient. What can you conclude, and what is this mnemonic?
options: You can rule in the disease; SpPIn
You can rule out the disease; SnNOut
The prevalence must be high; SnNOut
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: You can rule out the disease; SnNOut
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: SnNOut — a highly Sensitive test, when Negative, rules Out disease (good for screening). By contrast SpPIn — a highly Specific test, when Positive, rules In disease (good for confirmation).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Why does screening a low-prevalence population generate many false positives?
options: Because sensitivity falls as prevalence falls
Because PPV falls as prevalence falls, meaning more false positives relative to true positives
Because the test becomes less accurate over time
Because likelihood ratios change with prevalence
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Because PPV falls as prevalence falls, meaning more false positives relative to true positives
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are intrinsic, but PPV depends on prevalence: as prevalence falls, PPV falls (more false positives relative to true), which is why screening low-prevalence populations generates many false positives.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What does an odds ratio (OR) measure, and in which study design is it used?
options: Risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed; used in cohort studies
Odds of exposure in cases ÷ controls; used in case-control studies (approximates RR for rare disease)
Control event rate − treatment event rate; used in RCTs
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Odds of exposure in cases ÷ controls; used in case-control studies (approximates RR for rare disease)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The odds ratio measures the odds of exposure in cases ÷ controls and is used in case-control studies; it approximates the relative risk for rare diseases.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How is the number needed to treat (NNT) calculated, and how is it interpreted?
options: 1/ARR; the number of patients treated to prevent one outcome, where lower is better
Control rate − treatment rate; lower is better
Risk in exposed ÷ unexposed; >1 is harmful
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: 1/ARR; the number of patients treated to prevent one outcome, where lower is better
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: NNT = 1/ARR — the number of patients who need to be treated to prevent one outcome. A lower NNT is better. (1/absolute risk increase is the number needed to harm, NNH.)

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A drug trial reports an impressive relative risk reduction, but the absolute risk reduction is tiny. What is the concern?
options: The NNT will also be very low
Relative risk reduction is a proportional measure that can look impressive while the ARR is tiny — the 'spin' to watch for
The odds ratio must be wrong
The result cannot be statistically significant
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Relative risk reduction is a proportional measure that can look impressive while the ARR is tiny — the 'spin' to watch for
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Relative risk reduction is a proportional reduction that can look impressive even when the absolute risk reduction is tiny — the 'spin' to watch for when appraising trials.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A 95% confidence interval for a relative risk crosses 1. What does this indicate?
options: The result is not statistically significant
The sample size was too large
There was a type I error
The p-value must be less than 0.05
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The result is not statistically significant
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: If a 95% CI for RR/OR crosses 1 (or a difference crosses 0), the result is not statistically significant. A narrow CI indicates precision.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is a p-value?
options: The probability the null hypothesis is true
The probability the result (or more extreme) occurred by chance if the null were true; <0.05 is conventionally 'statistically significant'
The probability of a type II error
The effect size of the intervention
The proportion of patients who benefit
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The probability the result (or more extreme) occurred by chance if the null were true; <0.05 is conventionally 'statistically significant'
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: A p-value is the probability that the result (or a more extreme one) occurred by chance if the null hypothesis were true; <0.05 is the conventional (arbitrary) threshold for statistical significance.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A study concludes a treatment is effective, but in reality it has no effect. Which error has occurred?
options: Type I error (α) — a false positive, rejecting a true null
Type II error (β) — a false negative
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Type I error (α) — a false positive, rejecting a true null
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: A type I error (α) is a false positive — rejecting a true null hypothesis, i.e. concluding there is an effect that isn't real. A type II error (β) is the opposite — missing a real effect.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How can a study reduce the risk of a type II error (increase its power)?
options: Reduce the confidence interval width by chance
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Increase the sample size
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: A type II error (β) is a false negative — missing a real effect. Power = 1−β, and is increased by a larger sample size.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of the following is a recognised type of bias, and in which study type is recall bias particularly relevant?
options: Recall bias; particularly relevant in case-control studies
Random error; relevant in cohort studies
Publication bias; relevant in cross-sectional studies
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Recall bias; particularly relevant in case-control studies
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Bias is systematic error. Recall bias is particularly relevant in case-control studies (where cases recall exposures differently from controls). Other biases include selection, information/measurement, observer, lead-time, length-time and attrition bias.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A study finds that coffee drinkers have more lung cancer, but coffee drinkers also smoke more. Smoking is associated with both coffee and lung cancer. What is smoking acting as here, and how is it controlled?
options: A source of recall bias; controlled by blinding
A confounder; controlled by randomisation, matching, restriction, or multivariable adjustment
A type I error; controlled by a lower p-value
Attrition bias; controlled by intention-to-treat analysis
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: A confounder; controlled by randomisation, matching, restriction, or multivariable adjustment
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Smoking is a confounder — a third factor associated with both the exposure (coffee) and the outcome (lung cancer), distorting the link. Confounding is controlled by randomisation, matching, restriction, or multivariable adjustment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which methods specifically reduce bias in RCTs?
options: Randomisation, blinding, allocation concealment, and intention-to-treat analysis
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Randomisation, blinding, allocation concealment, and intention-to-treat analysis
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: In RCTs, bias is reduced by randomisation (balances confounders), blinding (single/double), allocation concealment, and intention-to-treat analysis.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: The 5 A's of the EBM process begin with forming a focused question. Which framework is used, and what is the correct order?
options: CASP; Acquire → Ask → Apply → Appraise → Assess
PICO; Ask → Acquire → Appraise → Apply → Assess
SnNOut; Assess → Ask → Apply → Acquire → Appraise
PICO; Acquire → Appraise → Ask → Assess → Apply
CASP; Ask → Assess → Acquire → Apply → Appraise
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: PICO; Ask → Acquire → Appraise → Apply → Assess
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The 5 A's are: Ask (form a focused PICO question — Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) → Acquire (search) → Appraise (critically appraise validity, e.g. CASP checklists) → Apply (to the patient, with their values) → Assess (evaluate outcome).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the core principle governing when a notifiable disease should be reported?
options: Notify only once laboratory confirmation is available
Notify on clinical suspicion alone — do not wait for laboratory confirmation
Notify only after the patient consents in writing
Notify only if the patient is admitted to hospital
Notify only after discussing with a microbiologist
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Notify on clinical suspicion alone — do not wait for laboratory confirmation
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The core principle is to notify on clinical suspicion alone; waiting for laboratory confirmation delays the public-health response.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Who holds the legal duty to notify a suspected notifiable disease?
options: The Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) — any GMC-registered doctor — with reasonable grounds for suspecting a notifiable disease
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP) — any GMC-registered doctor — with reasonable grounds for suspecting a notifiable disease
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The duty falls on the Registered Medical Practitioner (any GMC-registered doctor) who has reasonable grounds for suspecting a notifiable disease.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: To whom is a notifiable disease formally reported?
options: The 'Proper Officer' of the local authority (in practice, the local UKHSA Health Protection Team)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The 'Proper Officer' of the local authority (in practice, the local UKHSA Health Protection Team)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Notification is made to the 'Proper Officer' of the local authority, in practice the local UKHSA Health Protection Team.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the legal basis for the duty to notify, and is it optional?
options: GMC guidance only; it is advisory
The Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 — a statutory duty, not optional
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010 — a statutory duty, not optional
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The legal basis is the Public Health (Control of Disease) Act 1984 and the Health Protection (Notification) Regulations 2010, making notification a statutory duty, not optional.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A laboratory reports isolating Neisseria meningitidis from a blood culture. How does this affect the treating doctor's duty?
options: The lab report removes the doctor's duty to notify
The lab has a separate statutory duty, but a lab report does NOT remove the doctor's duty to notify on clinical suspicion — the two systems complement each other
Only the lab needs to notify in all cases
The doctor must wait for the lab before notifying
Neither party needs to notify once cultured
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The lab has a separate statutory duty, but a lab report does NOT remove the doctor's duty to notify on clinical suspicion — the two systems complement each other
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Diagnostic labs have a separate statutory duty to report specific notifiable organisms, but this does not remove the doctor's duty to notify on clinical suspicion; the two systems complement each other.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A GP strongly suspects meningococcal disease in a patient. By what route and within what time should this be notified?
options: Telephone the Health Protection Team within 24 hours
No notification until cultures confirm it
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Telephone the Health Protection Team within 24 hours
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Urgent cases such as meningococcal disease, measles and food-poisoning outbreaks are telephoned to the HPT within 24 hours, because there is often a critical window for control measures.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: How and within what timeframe is a routine notifiable case (e.g. TB, mumps, scarlet fever) reported?
options: Online / written notification form within 3 days
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Online / written notification form within 3 days
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Routine cases (TB, mumps, scarlet fever) are reported via an online / written notification form within 3 days.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: After telephoning an urgent notification within 24 hours, what additional step is still required?
options: All cases (including urgent) still need the written/online form within 3 days
A repeat phone call at 48 hours
A letter to the patient's employer
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: All cases (including urgent) still need the written/online form within 3 days
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: Urgent cases are phoned within 24 h, but all cases — including urgent ones — still require the written/online form within 3 days.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which group of diseases falls under the vaccine-preventable / childhood notifiable category?
options: Measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis, diphtheria, tetanus, polio
Rabies, malaria, viral haemorrhagic fevers, brucellosis
TB, Legionnaires' disease, SARS, invasive group A strep
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis, diphtheria, tetanus, polio
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The vaccine-preventable / childhood group comprises measles, mumps, rubella, pertussis (whooping cough), diphtheria, tetanus and polio (acute poliomyelitis).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of the following is a notifiable GI / food & water disease?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Typhoid & paratyphoid (enteric fever)
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The GI / food & water notifiable group includes food poisoning, cholera, typhoid & paratyphoid (enteric fever), dysentery and acute hepatitis A-E.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which of these is in the respiratory / environmental notifiable group?
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Legionnaires' disease
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The respiratory / environmental notifiable group includes TB, Legionnaires' disease, SARS, COVID-19 and invasive group A strep.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: A patient is diagnosed with an MRSA bloodstream infection. Is this statutorily notifiable?
options: Yes — it must be phoned within 24 hours
No — MRSA / Staph aureus has separate surveillance, not statutory notification
Yes — via the online form within 3 days
Yes — it is in the severe bacterial group
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: No — MRSA / Staph aureus has separate surveillance, not statutory notification
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: MRSA / Staph aureus, along with C. difficile and CJD, have separate surveillance rather than statutory notification — the classic trap. HIV is also not statutorily notifiable (confidential surveillance).

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Is HIV a statutorily notifiable disease in this framework?
options: Yes — it is notifiable within 24 hours
No — HIV is not statutorily notifiable; it has confidential surveillance
Yes — it is notifiable within 3 days
Yes — it is in the zoonotic group
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: No — HIV is not statutorily notifiable; it has confidential surveillance
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: HIV is not statutorily notifiable; it is monitored through confidential surveillance, making it part of the non-notifiable trap alongside MRSA, C. difficile and CJD.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: According to the 'all-hazards' catch-all principle, what should an RMP notify beyond the formal disease list?
options: Only diseases on the statutory list, never anything else
Any infection or contamination (including non-listed/emerging infections and chemical/radiation hazards) that presents, or could present, significant harm to human health
Only conditions affecting more than 100 people
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Any infection or contamination (including non-listed/emerging infections and chemical/radiation hazards) that presents, or could present, significant harm to human health
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The all-hazards principle means the duty isn't limited to the listed diseases: an RMP should notify any infection or contamination, including non-listed/emerging infections and chemical/radiation hazards (e.g. a novel pathogen, a cluster, or carbon monoxide poisoning), that could significantly harm human health.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: Which scenario best illustrates the 'all-hazards' principle in action?
options: Notifying a confirmed case of measles
Notifying parvovirus B19 in a contact of a pregnant woman, even though it's not on the formal list
Notifying scarlet fever via the routine form
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Notifying parvovirus B19 in a contact of a pregnant woman, even though it's not on the formal list
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: An example of the all-hazards principle is notifying parvovirus B19 in a contact of a pregnant woman, despite it not being on the formal statutory list.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: What is the underlying public-health rationale for the notification system?
options: To bill patients for infectious diseases
Surveillance, outbreak detection, contact tracing, and implementing control measures to prevent further spread
To provide individual treatment to the index patient only
To register diseases for research consent
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Surveillance, outbreak detection, contact tracing, and implementing control measures to prevent further spread
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: The purpose of notification is population protection through surveillance, outbreak detection, contact tracing and control measures — not individual treatment.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: After a meningococcal disease notification, which prophylaxis step is used to break the chain of transmission in close contacts?
options: No prophylaxis is given to contacts
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: Ciprofloxacin for meningococcal contacts
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: After notification, breaking the chain includes contact tracing and prophylaxis — vaccination or antibiotics for contacts, e.g. ciprofloxacin for meningococcal contacts — plus environmental investigation where relevant.

conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.question: After notification, who takes over the epidemiological work, and what remains the doctor's job?
options: The doctor does all the epidemiology; the HPT does nothing
The HPT takes over the epidemiological work; the doctor's job is the prompt, suspicion-based notification
The laboratory leads contact tracing; the doctor treats only
The patient coordinates their own contact tracing
NHS England performs the notification on the doctor's behalf
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.answer: The HPT takes over the epidemiological work; the doctor's job is the prompt, suspicion-based notification
conditions__PUBLIC HEALTH & EVIDENCE-BAS.explanation: After notification the Health Protection Team takes over the epidemiological work (contact tracing, prophylaxis, environmental investigation); the doctor's job is the prompt, suspicion-based notification.
